Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 1:

(p-590)Surat al-Naml

Surat al-Naml is Meccan, and it has ninety-three verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ta-Sin. These are the verses of the Qur'an and of a clear Book.﴾ That is: the verses of a clear Book. "Those" (tilka) is a pointer to the verses of the surah. The "clear Book" (al-kitab al-mubin) is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh), and its verses are that everything that exists has been inscribed in it, so it makes clear to those who look into it its verses. Or [it means] the Qur'an and its verses are that it makes clear what has been deposited in it of sciences and wisdoms. On this reading, its being conjoined to the Qur'an is like the conjoining of one of two attributes to the other, as in the expression "this is the act of the generous and the bountiful." The word "Book" is indefinite so that it may be more majestic for it. It has also been said: he made "Book" indefinite here and definite in al-Hijr, and made "Qur'an" definite here and indefinite there, because "Qur'an" and "Book" are both proper names for what was sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ) and also descriptive terms for it, since it is recited (yuqra') and written (yuktab). So wherever it comes with the definite form, it is the proper name, and wherever it comes with the indefinite form, it is the descriptive term.

"Guidance and good news" (﴿هُدًى وبُشْرى﴾) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl, a grammatical state or condition) of *āyāt* (آياتٍ, "signs"), meaning: guiding and bringing good news. Its governing element is what the demonstrative *tilka* (تِلْكَ, "those") contains of the sense of pointing (ishārah). It may also be in the genitive, as a substitute (badal, an appositive replacement) for *kitāb* (كِتابٍ, "Book") or as a qualifier (ṣifah, an adjective) of it. It may be in the nominative, meaning "it is guidance and good news," or as a substitute for *āyāt*, or as a second predicate (khabar, the predicate of a sentence) following another predicate for *tilka*, meaning: "those are signs, and guiding from error and bringing good news of Paradise." It was also said: "guidance for all of creation, and good news," and the phrase ﴿لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("for the believers") is specific to them alone. (p-591)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 3:

﴿Those who establish the prayer﴾ (yuqimuna al-salat) — they persist in its obligatory acts (fara'id) and its recommended acts (sunan). ﴿And who give the zakat﴾ — they pay the zakat (zakat) of their wealth. ﴿And they, in the Hereafter, they are certain﴾ — this is part of the relative clause (silat al-mawsul). It is also possible that the relative clause ends at this point, and that this sentence is a fresh statement (isti'naf), as if it were said: "These are the ones who believe and do righteous deeds, by establishing the prayer and giving the zakat; they are the ones certain of the Hereafter." This is supported by the fact that he formed a nominal sentence and repeated in it the subject, which is "hum" (they), until its meaning becomes: "None are certain of the Hereafter with true certainty except these who combine faith and righteous action," because the fear of the consequence drives them to bear hardships.

Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter—We have made their deeds appealing to them by creating desire, so that they see those deeds as good, just as He said: ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made appealing to him, so that he sees it as good...?﴾ [Fatir: 8]. ﴿So they wander aimlessly﴾ (ya'mahun), hesitating in their misguidance, just as the state of one who has lost his way is.

Those are the ones for whom is the worst of punishment: killing and capture on the day of Badr, for what they had done of evil deeds. And in the Hereafter they are the greatest losers: the most extreme of people in loss, because if they had believed they would have been among the witnesses over all the nations, but they lost that along with the loss of salvation and the reward of Allah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 6:

﴿And indeed, you are being given the Qur'an﴾: you are being granted it and having it imparted to you, ﴿from the presence of One who is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾: from the side of some Wise One and some Knowing One, and this is the meaning of their being indefinite (nakir). This verse is a foundation and preparation for what he intends to recount after it of stories, and of the subtleties of His wisdom and the fine points of His knowledge that are in those stories.

**﴿Idh﴾** is in the accusative case, governed by **udhkur** (remember). It is as if he had said: "Recount, following upon that, from the signs of His wisdom and knowledge, the story of Musa, peace be upon him." **﴿Qala Musa li-ahlihi﴾** (Musa said to his family): to his wife and those with him, when he was traveling from Madyan toward Misr. "**Imkuthu inni anastu**" (Stay here, for I have perceived) means: I saw **﴿a fire, I will bring you from it news﴾** about the condition of the road, because he had lost his way. **﴿Aw atikum bi-shihabin﴾** (or I will bring you a brand): the reader **Kufi** (of the Kufan reading tradition) reads it with **tanwin** (nunation, the "-n" ending on the noun) meaning a blazing flame, i.e., a lit brand of fire (**qabas**), and it is either in apposition (**badal**) or an adjective (**sifa**). Others read **bi-shihabi qabasin** (with an **idafa**, the construct phrase "a brand of a live coal"), because a brand may be a live coal or may not be one. There is no contradiction between his saying **﴿sa-atikum﴾** (I will bring you) here and "**la'alli atikum**" (perhaps I will bring you) in the other narration, although one expresses hope and the other certainty. This is because the one who hopes, when his hope is strong, says "I will do such-and-such" and "such-and-such will happen," even though he allows for failure. The use of the particle **sin** of futurity (**sa-**) is a promise to his family that he will bring it to them, even if he is delayed or the distance is great. The use of **aw** (or) is because he based his hope on the fact that if he did not obtain all of his needs, he would not lose one of them: either guidance on the road or taking a brand from the fire. He did not know that he would obtain both of his complete needs from the fire, which were the glory of this world and the Hereafter. The difference in wording between these two passages, while the story is one, is evidence for the permissibility of transmitting a report **bi-l-ma'na** (by its meaning, not its exact words), and for the permissibility of a marriage contract without using the word **tazawwuj** (marriage). **﴿La'allakum tasta-lunа﴾** (that you may warm yourselves) means: that you may warm yourselves at the fire against the cold that has afflicted you. The **ta'** (ط) is a substitution for the **ta'** of the form **ifta'ala**, for the sake of the **sad** (ص).

(p. 592)

﴿So when he came to it﴾, that is, to the fire which he had seen, Moses was called: ﴿that blessed is﴾. The word "an" here is the lightened form of the heavy (an-)particle, and its implied sense is: he was called with the words "blessed is." The pronoun is a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and this usage is permitted without a replacement (ʿiwaḍ), although al-Zamakhshari prohibited it, because his saying "blessed is" is a supplication (du'a'), and supplication differs from other speech in many rulings. Or the "an" is explanatory (mufassira), because in the calling (al-nida') there is the meaning of saying; that is: it was said to him "blessed is," i.e., sanctified, or made to contain blessing and goodness. ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it﴾, that is: blessed is whoever is in the place of the fire, namely the angels, and whoever is around its place, namely Moses, because of a religious matter that occurred there, which is God's speaking to Moses, appointing him as a prophet, and manifesting miracles upon him. ﴿And glory be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾: this is part of what was called out; He declared Himself far above what is unfitting for Him, such as likeness (tashbih) and other things.

﴿Yā Mūsā, innahu anā Allāhu al-ʿAzīzu al-Ḥakīm﴾ (ﷺ not applicable). "O Musa, indeed it is I, Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise."

The pronoun in *innahu* (ḍamīr al-sha'n, the pronoun of the matter, referring to the situation or the subject being announced) is *li-l-sha'n* (refers to the matter at hand). *Anā Allāhu* is a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence) and *khabar* (predicate). *Al-ʿAzīzu al-Ḥakīm* are two *ṣifatān* (qualifying adjectives) of the *khabar*.

Alternatively, the pronoun refers to what is implied by what precedes it, meaning: indeed the One speaking to you is "I." *Allāhu* is a *bayān* (explicative apposition, clarifying the term before it) for *anā*, and *al-ʿAzīzu al-Ḥakīm* are two *ṣifatān* of the clarified term. This is a *tamhīd* (preparation, introduction) for what He intended to manifest through Musa's hand of the miracle. (p-593)

﴿And throw down your staff﴾, so that you may know your miracle and be reassured by it. It is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to *būrika* (be blessed), because the meaning is: he was called out that *būrika man fī al-nār* (blessed is whoever is in the fire) and that *an alqi ʿaṣāka* (throw down your staff). Both are an explanation (tafsir) of *nūdiya* (he was called). The meaning is: it was said to him, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire," and it was said to him, "Throw down your staff." This is supported by what is mentioned in Surah al-Qasas: ﴿And that throw down your staff﴾ [al-Qasas: 31], after His saying ﴿That O Musa, indeed I am Allah﴾ [al-Qasas: 30], with the explanatory particle (harf al-tafsir) repeated.

﴿So when he saw it moving﴾: *tahtazzu*, it moves, is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in *raʾāhā* (he saw it). ﴿as if it were a snake﴾: *jānn*, a small snake, is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *tahtazzu*. ﴿he turned back﴾: Musa turned away, *mudbiran*, turning his back to it, out of fear that the snake would leap upon him. ﴿and did not return﴾: he did not look back, or he did not return. It is said: "So-and-so *ʿaqqaba* (returned)" when he turned back to fight after having fled. Then he was called: ﴿O Musa, do not fear. Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾ (*innī lā yakhāfu ladayya al-mursalūn*). That is: the messengers do not fear in My presence while I am addressing them, or: the messengers do not fear in My presence, apart from others.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 11:

﴿Except one who has done wrong﴾ That is: but whoever among others has done wrong, because the prophets do not do wrong. Or: but whoever among them has done wrong, meaning one of the messengers who slipped and acted contrary to what I had permitted him, of the kind that is permissible for prophets, such as the lapses of Adam, Yunus, Dawud and Sulayman, upon them be peace. ﴿Then substitutes good﴾ That is: follows with repentance ﴿after evil﴾, a slip. ﴿Then indeed I am Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾: I accept his repentance, forgive his slip, and show him mercy, so I fulfil his hope. It seems to be an allusion to what Musa said when he killed the Egyptian: ﴿My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, so forgive me.﴾ So He forgave him. [al-Qasas: 16]

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 12:

﴿And insert your hand into your bosom﴾ (jayb), the opening of your shirt, ﴿and bring it out; it will come out white﴾, luminous, overpowering the light of the sun, ﴿without harm﴾ (su') – leprosy. And "white" and "without harm" are two circumstantial clauses (hal). ﴿Among the nine signs﴾ is a new (independent) statement, and "among" (fi) is connected to an omitted element, meaning: go among the nine signs; or, "and cast your staff, and insert your hand" is within the category of the nine signs ﴿to Pharaoh and his people﴾. "To" (ila) is connected to an omitted element, meaning: sent to Pharaoh ﴿Indeed they were a people of defiance﴾ – going outside the command of Allah, disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 13:

﴿So when Our signs came to them﴾, i.e., Our miracles, ﴿clearly visible (mubṣira)﴾ — this is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: manifest and evident. The seeing (al-ibṣār) is ascribed to them (the signs), though in reality it belongs to those who contemplate them, because of their engagement with them through looking and reflection. Or, they are treated as though they see and therefore guide, since the blind cannot find guidance, let alone guide others. From this is the expression "a blind word" (kalima 'amyā') and "a crooked word" (kalima 'awrā'), because a good word guides and a bad word misleads. ﴿They said, "This is manifest sorcery (siḥr mubīn)"﴾, clear to whoever contemplates it. The text sets "clearly visible (mubṣira)" in contrast with "manifest (mubīn)."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 14:

﴿And they denied them﴾. It has been said: "Denial (al-judud) only occurs from knowledge on the part of the one who denies, and this is not correct, because denial (al-judud) is rejection (al-inkar), and rejection of a thing may occur out of ignorance of it, and it may occur after recognition, out of obstinacy." Thus it is mentioned in Sharh al-Ta'wilat. And it is mentioned in al-Diwan: one says "jahada haqqahu" and "jahada bi-haqqihi" with the same meaning. The waw in ﴿and they were certain of them﴾ is for the circumstantial clause (lil-hal), and there is a concealed pronoun after it (qad ba'daha mudmara). And al-istiyqan (certainty) is more emphatic than al-iyqan. ﴿Their souls﴾, i.e., they denied with their tongues and were certain of them in their hearts and inner consciences. ﴿Out of wrongdoing﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "jahadu," and what wrongdoing is more grievous than the wrongdoing of one who is certain that they are signs from Allah, and then calls them clear magic? ﴿And arrogance﴾, i.e., haughtiness, refusing to believe in what Musa brought. ﴿So see how was the end of the corrupters﴾, which here is drowning, and burning elsewhere.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 27, verse 15:

﴿And We certainly gave﴾ we bestowed upon ﴿Dawud and Sulayman knowledge﴾ a portion of knowledge, or abundant, lofty knowledge. What is meant is the knowledge of religion and judgment. ﴿And they both said: "Praise be to Allah, who has preferred us over many of His believing servants."﴾ The verses are a proof for us against the Mu'tazila (the rationalist theological school) regarding their doctrine of *tark al-aslah* (that God must always do what is best for His servants). Here something is omitted so that the conjunction *wa* (و, "and") can correctly coordinate with it. Were it not for the assumption of the omitted element, the proper particle would be *fa* (ف, "so/then"), as in your saying, "I gave him, and he gave thanks." Its implied meaning is: "We gave them both knowledge, so they acted upon it, taught it, and recognized the true due of this blessing, and they said: 'Praise be to Allah, who has preferred us.'" The "many" who are preferred over are those who were not given knowledge, or who were not given the like of their knowledge. In it there is the implication that they were preferred over many, and many were preferred over them. The verse is evidence of the nobility of knowledge, the precedence of its bearers and its people, and that the blessing of knowledge is among the greatest blessings, and that whoever is given it has been given excellence over many of Allah's servants. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called the scholars "the heirs of the prophets" only because of their closeness to them in nobility and rank, since they are the custodians of that with which the prophets were sent. In it also is that, because of this excellent blessing, they are obligated to praise Allah for what they have been given, and that the scholar should believe that if he is preferred over many, then the like of them has also been preferred over him. How excellent is the saying of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "Every person is more knowledgeable than Umar" (may Allah be pleased with him)!

﴿And Solomon inherited from David﴾: he inherited prophethood (*nubuwwah*) and kingship (*mulk*), to the exclusion of the rest of his sons, and they were nineteen in number. Some said: he was given prophethood like his father, so it is as though he inherited it from him. Otherwise, prophethood is not inherited.

﴿And he said: O people, we have been taught the speech (*mantiq*) of birds﴾: to make known the blessing of God, the Exalted, to acknowledge its magnitude, and to call people to belief through mention of the miracle, which is knowledge of the speech of birds. *Mantiq* is everything that is vocalized, whether a single sound or a composed utterance, whether it conveys meaning or not. Solomon, peace be upon him, understood them just as some of them understand one another. It is narrated that a turtle-dove cooed, and he reported that it was saying: "Would that these creatures had not been created." A peacock called, and he said it was saying: "As you judge, so you will be judged." A hoopoe called, and he said it was saying: "Seek forgiveness from God, O sinners." A swallow called, and he said it was saying: "Send forth good deeds, you will find them." A vulture called, and he said it was saying: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High, filling His heaven and His earth." A dove called, and he reported that it was saying: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High." He said the kite says: "Everything perishes except God." The partridge says: "Whoever keeps silent is safe." The rooster says: "In distance from people there is intimacy." The frog says: "Glory be to my Lord, the Holy."

﴿And we have been given of everything﴾: what is meant is the abundance of what was given, as one says, "So-and-so knows everything." Similar is ﴿and she [the Queen of Sheba] has been given of everything﴾ [al-Naml: 23].

﴿Indeed, this is clearly a great favour﴾: this statement is made by way of thanks, like the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I am the master of the children of Adam, and I say this not out of boasting." That is, I say this statement as an expression of gratitude, not of pride. The *nūn* in *ʿullimnā* (we have been taught) and *ūtīnā* (we have been given) is the *nūn* of the single one who is obeyed (*nūn al-wāḥid al-muṭāʿ*). Since he was an obeyed king, he addressed those under his authority in the state in which he was. Arrogance is not a necessary consequence of this.

﴿And were gathered﴾ and assembled ﴿for Sulayman his soldiers, of the jinn and the humans and the birds﴾. It is narrated that his encampment was a hundred farsakhs by a hundred farsakhs (a farsakh being a unit of distance of about three miles). Twenty-five farsakhs were for the jinn, twenty-five for the humans, twenty-five for the birds, and twenty-five for the wild beasts. He had a thousand tents of glass set on wooden poles, in which were three hundred wives (mankuha) and seven hundred concubines (suriyya). The jinn had woven for him a carpet of gold and silk, one farsakh by one farsakh. His pulpit (minbar) was placed in its centre, and it was made of gold and silver. Around them were the people, and around the people were the jinn and the devils. The birds shaded him with their wings so that the sun would not fall upon him, and the gentle east wind (rih al-saba) lifted him and carried him a month's journey. It is also narrated that he would command the violent wind to carry him, and command the gentle breeze to move him along. Then Allah the Exalted revealed to him, while he was travelling between heaven and earth: "I have increased your kingdom so that no one speaks a word except that the wind casts it into your hearing." It is related that he passed by a ploughman and said: "The family of Dawud has indeed been given a great kingdom," and the wind cast it into his ear. So he descended, walked to the ploughman and said: "I have come to you so that you do not wish for what you have no power over." The ploughman said: "A single glorification (tasbih) that Allah the Exalted accepts is better than what the family of Dawud has been given." ﴿Then they were held in order﴾: their first is restrained upon their last, meaning the vanguard (sulaf) of the army is halted until those behind them catch up, so that they remain gathered together; and this is because of the great multitude. Al-wazʿ (from the root wa-za-ʿa, here "restraining" or "holding back") means restraint; and from it is the saying of Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him: "What the ruler restrains is more than what the Qur'an restrains."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 18:

﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants﴾ That is: they proceeded until, when they reached the valley of the ants, which is a valley in al-Sham (Greater Syria) abounding in ants. The verb is construed with ʿalā (upon), because their coming was from above, so the particle of elevation (ḥarf al-istiʿlāʾ) was used. ﴿An ant said﴾ — a lame ant, called Ṭākhiyah or Mundhirah. It is related from Qatadah that he entered Kufa, and the people gathered around him, and he said: "Ask me whatever you wish." Abu Hanifah (may Allah be pleased with him), who was then a young man, asked him whether the ant of Sulayman was male or female, and he was struck dumb. Abu Hanifah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "It was female." He was asked: "By what did you know that?" He said: "By His saying ﴿an ant said﴾. Had it been male, it would have said 'an ant said' (qāla namlatun, with the masculine verb)." This is because the ant (al-namlah) is like the dove (al-ḥamāmah) in that it applies to both male and female, so they are distinguished by a marker, as in the saying "ḥamāmah dhakar" (a male dove) and "ḥamāmah unthā" (a female dove), and "huwa" and "hiya."

﴿O you ants, enter your dwellings﴾. He did not say "udkhulna" (feminine plural imperative), because when He made them speaking and the ants as those addressed, as is the case with rational beings, He applied to them the form of address used for them. ﴿Lest Sulayman and his hosts crush you﴾ — lest they break you. Al-ḥaṭm means breaking. This is a new, independent prohibition. Outwardly it is a prohibition to Sulayman against crushing, but in reality it is a prohibition to the ants against coming out and standing (in the open), following the pattern of "lā arayannaka hahuna" (I should not see you here), meaning: do not be present at this place. It was said that it is a response to a command, but this is weak, since the emphatic nūn (in yaḥṭimannakum) repels it, for that is a necessity of poetry. ﴿Sulayman and his hosts﴾ — it was said that she meant: "Lest the hosts of Sulayman crush you," but she used the more eloquent expression. ﴿And they do not perceive﴾ — they do not know your place; that is, had they perceived, they would not have done it. She said this by way of excuse, describing Sulayman and his hosts with justice. Sulayman heard her words from three miles away.

﴿So he smiled, laughing at her words﴾, amazed at her caution, at her being guided to what benefits her kind, and at her advice to the ants; or joyful at the manifestation of his justice. "Laughing" is a emphatic state (hal), because tabassama (smiled) means dahika (laughed), and most of the laughter of the prophets was smiling; so said al-Zajjaj. ﴿And he said, "My Lord, inspire me﴾, meaning, enable me (alhimni). Its reality is "restrain me (kuffani) from things except from giving thanks for Your blessing," ﴿to be grateful for Your blessing which You have bestowed upon me﴾, namely prophethood, kingship and knowledge, ﴿and upon my parents﴾, because bestowing blessing upon one's parents is bestowing blessing upon the child, ﴿and that I may do righteous deeds which please You﴾ for the rest of my life. "And admit me by Your mercy" and "admit me to Paradise by Your mercy," not by the merit of my good deeds, since no one enters Paradise except by His mercy, as has come in the hadith.

﴿among Your righteous servants﴾, i.e., among the company of Your messenger prophets, or along with Your righteous servants. It is narrated that the ant perceived the sound of the troops, not knowing that they were in the air. So Sulayman commanded the wind, and it stood still, lest they be frightened, until they entered their dwellings. Then he made the supplication.

(p-598)

And He inspected the birds and said, ﴿What is the matter with me? I do not see the hoopoe; or is he among the absent?﴾ Makki, Ali and Asim, and others, read *yā'* with sukūn (as *mā lī*). *Al-tafaqqud* means seeking what has gone missing from you. ﴿I do not see the hoopoe; or is he among the absent?﴾ *Am* here means *bal* (rather). The meaning is: he searched among the birds and did not find the hoopoe among them, so he said, "What is the matter with me that I do not see him?" meaning that he does not see him though he is present, because of some screen that concealed him or some other reason. Then it became clear to him that the hoopoe was absent, so he turned away from that and began to say, "Rather, he is absent."

It is related that when Sulayman, peace be upon him, went on pilgrimage, he set out for Yemen and reached Sana'a at the time of midday. He dismounted to pray but found no water. The hoopoe was his *qunaqinah* (the one who guides him to water), and it could see water beneath the earth as one sees water in a glass, and the devils would extract the water. So he searched for it for this reason. It is also related that a ray of sunlight fell upon the head of Sulayman, so he looked and found the place of the hoopoe empty. He summoned the *arīf al-ṭayr* (chief or overseer of the birds), who is the eagle (*al-nasr*), and asked him about it, but he did not have knowledge of it. (p-599) Then he said to the lord of the birds, who is the falcon (*al-'uqāb*), "Bring him to me." So it rose up, looked, and saw the hoopoe approaching. It made for him and adjured him by God, so it released him. When he drew near to Sulayman, he let down his tail and wings, dragging them along the ground, and said, "O Prophet of God, remember your standing before the Lord." Sulayman trembled and pardoned him.

﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment﴾ by plucking out his feathers and casting him into the sun, or by separating him from his beloved mate, or by compelling him to serve his peers, or by imprisoning him with his opposites. It is related from some of them: "The narrowest of prisons is the company of opposites." Or by placing him in a cage, or by throwing him before the ants so that they eat him. Punishing the hoopoe (hudhud) was permissible for him because of the benefit he saw in it, just as slaughtering animals and birds is permissible for eating and other benefits. When the birds were subjected to him, the subjection was not complete except through discipline and governance. ﴿Or I will surely slaughter him, or he must bring me a clear authority﴾ with the heavy nun (al-nun al-thaqilah, the emphatic nun), to match his saying لَأُعَذِّبَنَّهُ. The supporting nun (nun al-'imad, the nun inserted before the pronoun ي) is omitted for lightness. "لَيَأْتِيَنَّنِي" with two nuns is the reading of Makki: the first is for emphasis and the second is the supporting nun. ﴿With a clear authority﴾ means with a proof for him in which there is a manifest excuse for his absence. The difficulty is that he swore to one of three things. Two of them are his own action, and there is no discussion about them. The third is the action of the hoopoe, and this is problematic, because from where did he know that it would bring an authority, that he said: "By God, he will surely bring me an authority"? Its answer is that the meaning of his speech is: one of the matters will certainly occur. That is, if the bringing of an authority occurs, there will be no punishment or slaughter; and if it does not occur, one of the two will. And in this there is no claim of knowledge.

﴿So he remained﴾ the hoopoe (al-Hudhud), after Sulayman had searched for him, and with a damma on the kaf (فَمُكْثَ) by everyone other than ʿĀṣim, Sahl and Yaʿqūb. The two are dialectal variants (lughatān). ﴿not long﴾: that is, a stay that was not long, or not a long time, like His saying ﴿soon﴾. He described his stay as brief to indicate his haste out of fear of Sulayman. When he returned, Sulayman asked him what he had encountered during his absence. ﴿He said, "I have comprehended﴾: I have learned something from all its aspects ﴿that you have not comprehended﴾. God inspired the hoopoe, and so he confronted Sulayman with these words, despite what Sulayman had been given of the excellence of prophethood and abundant knowledge, as a trial for him in his knowledge. In this is evidence against the claim of the Rafiḍa (the Rafidites, a term for the Shi'a who reject the first caliphs) that the Imam is not hidden from anything and that no one in his time is more knowledgeable than him. ﴿And I have come to you from Saba'﴾: Abu ʿAmr read it as non-diptote (ghayr munṣaraf), and made it the name of a tribe or a city. Others read it with tanwin, making it the name of a clan or of a great forefather. ﴿with certain news﴾: al-naba' (news) is information that has significance. His saying ﴿from Saba' with news﴾ is one of the beauties of speech, called al-badīʿ (rhetorical embellishment), and it is excellent and wondrous both in wording and in meaning here. Consider that if "bi-nabaʾin" were replaced with "bi-khabarin," the meaning would still be sound, but, as it came, it is more correct, because of the additional nuance in naba' which the description of the situation corresponds to.

"Indeed, I found a woman ruling over them" (﴿إنِّي وجَدْتُ امْرَأةً﴾). She was Bilqis, daughter of Sharahil. Her father was king of the land of Yemen, and he had no son besides her, so she prevailed over the kingship. She and her people were Magians (majus), worshipping the sun. The pronoun in ﴿تَمْلِكُهُمْ﴾ ("ruling over them") refers to Saba', taken as referring to the people, or alternatively to the inhabitants of the city. ﴿وَأُوتِيَتْ﴾ ("and she has been given") is a circumstantial clause (hal), with the qualification "qad" implied as "muqaddarah" (i.e., with qad understood, meaning "having been given"). ﴿مِن كُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ ("of everything") means of the means of worldly life that befit her station. ﴿وَلَها عَرْشٌ﴾ ("and she has a throne") means a seat/couch (sarir), ﴿عَظِيمٌ﴾ ("great") means large. It is said that it was eighty cubits by eighty cubits, and its height in the air was eighty cubits. It was made of gold and silver, encrusted with all kinds of jewels, its legs were of red and green ruby, pearls and emerald, and on it were seven chambers, each chamber having a locked door. He (Sulayman) regarded her state as small in comparison with his own state, and thus he considered her throne great. Allah the Exalted concealed that from Sulayman for a benefit He saw in it, just as He concealed the place of Yusuf from Ya'qub, peace be upon them both.

She found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah, and Satan has made their deeds appear fair to them and barred them from the path,

﴿so they are not guided﴾. That is, the path of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness). ﴿They are not guided﴾ to the truth. It is not far-fetched that the hoopoe (al-Hudhud) was guided to knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, the obligation to prostrate to Him, and the prohibition of prostrating to the sun, by inspiration (ilham) from Allah. He inspired it, and other birds and all animals, with subtle knowledge (ma'arif latifa) that sound-minded intelligent people barely arrive at.

**﴿ألا يَسْجُدُوا﴾** with the **tashdid** (doubled lam, i.e. the reading with the shaddah), meaning: "so He barred them from the way, so that they would not prostrate." The preposition (*al-jarr*, here *li*, "so that") is elided together with *an* (the "that" particle), and the nun of *an* is assimilated into the lam (*idgham*, assimilation). It is also permissible for *la* to be a superfluous particle (*zā'idah*), in which case the meaning is: "they are not guided to prostrate." With the **takhfif** (single lam, the lightened reading), Yazid and 'Ali read it, and its analysis is: "*Ala yā hā'ulā'i-sjudū*" ("Unquestionably, O people, prostrate!"). Here *Ala* (*alā*) is the particle of alerting (*li-l-tanbīh*), *yā* is the particle of calling, and the one being addressed is omitted. Whoever reads with the tashdid does not stop except at **"al-'arsh al-'azīm"** (the Mighty Throne). Whoever reads with the takhfif stops at **"fa-hum lā yahtadūn"** (so they are not guided), then begins with **"Alā yā-usjudū"**. The prostration of recitation (*sajdat al-tilāwah*) is obligatory in both readings together, unlike what al-Zajjaj says, that prostration is not obligatory with the tashdid, because the places of prostration are either a command to perform it, or a praise of the one who performs it, or a censure of the one who abandons it, and one of the two readings is a command while the other is a censure of the one who abandons it.

﴿لِلَّهِ الَّذِي يُخْرِجُ الخَبْءَ﴾ *[To Allah, who brings forth the hidden thing]*. He named the hidden thing (*al-makhbū'*) by the verbal noun (*khab'*). ﴿فِي السَماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾ *[in the heavens and the earth]*. Qatadah said: the hidden thing of the sky is the rain, and the hidden thing of the earth is the vegetation.

﴿وَيَعْلَمُ ما تُخْفُونَ وما تُعْلِنُونَ﴾ *[and He knows what you conceal and what you disclose]*. With the **ta'** (second person, "you") in both verbs, read by 'Ali and Hafs.

Surah 27, verse 26:

﴿Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Lord of the Great Throne.﴾ The hoopoe's description of God's throne as "great" is an exaltation of it in relation to all that He created of the heavens and the earth, while its description of Bilqis's throne as "great" is an exaltation of it in comparison to the thrones of the kings of her kind. Up to here is the speech of the hoopoe, when it finished its speech.

ÿ"Solomon said to the hoopoe, ﴿We shall see whether you have told the truth, or whether you were one of the liars.﴾ "Nazara" here is from the sense of "nazar", which is reflection and consideration. The phrasing ﴿أصَدَقْتَ أمْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الكاذِبِينَ﴾ (whether you have told the truth, or whether you were one of the liars) is more eloquent than ﴿أمْ كَذَبْتَ﴾ (or whether you have lied), because if he was known to be among the liars, he was certainly a liar, and if he was a liar, he would be accused of lying in what he reported, and so he would not be trusted.

Then Solomon wrote a letter whose text was: "From the servant of Allah, Solomon son of Dawud, to Bilqis, queen of Sheba. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Peace upon whoever follows the guidance. To proceed: do not exalt yourselves against me, and come to me in submission." He sealed it with musk, stamped it with his ring, and said to the hoopoe...

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 28:

﴿Go with this letter of mine, and throw it to them.﴾ Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Hamzah read the ha' (of fa-alqihu) with sukun, as a lightening (takhfif). Yazid, Qaloon and Ya'qub read it with a rapid, partial vowel (ikhtilas), a kasrah, so that the kasrah points to the omitted ya'. Others read "fa-alqihi" with the ya' affirmed. ﴿to them﴾: to Bilqis and her people, because he had mentioned them along with her in His words, ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun﴾ [al-Naml: 24]. For this reason he framed the address in the letter in the plural form. ﴿Then withdraw from them﴾: move away from them to a nearby place, close enough that you can see them while they cannot see you, so that what they say may be within earshot of you. ﴿and see what they will return﴾: what answer they will give back. So the hoopoe took the letter in its beak, entered upon her through a window (kuwwah), and dropped the letter onto her chest while she was asleep, then hid himself in the window. She awoke startled, or the troops came around her; he hovered for a while and then let the letter fall into her lap. She was a reader, and when she saw the seal (al-Khatam)...

﴿She said﴾ to her people, humbled and fearful: ﴿O chiefs, indeed I﴾ (Madani reads it with a fatha on the ya', i.e. "innī" with the vowel changed; here it is the reading of the Madinan reciter) ﴿have been delivered a noble letter﴾, meaning one whose content and what is in it is good, or one that is sealed. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The honour of a letter is its sealing." It is also said: whoever writes a letter to his brother and does not seal it has treated him with contempt. Or it is introduced with "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," or because it comes from a noble angel.

It is an explanation of what was thrown to her, as if when she said, ﴿Indeed, a noble letter has been delivered to me﴾ [al-Naml: 29], she was asked, "From whom is it, and what is it?" and she said, "Indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it is: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [such-and-such, and such-and-such]." (p. 603)

Here "an" in "allā ta'lū" is explanatory (mufassira), like His saying ﴿And the chiefs among them went forth, saying: Walk on﴾ [Sad: 6], meaning: "that is, walk." ﴿And come to me in submission﴾ meaning believing or submitting. The letters of the prophets are built on brevity and conciseness.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 32:**

﴿She said: "O chiefs, advise me in my matter."﴾ Give me your opinion concerning the affair that has come upon me. The *fatwa* (a formal legal or considered answer given on a matter) is the response given regarding an incident. The word is derived, by way of metaphor (*isti'arah*), from *fita'* (youthfulness of age). What is meant here by *fatwa* is giving counsel with what they hold of opinion. Her purpose in returning to consult them is to put their minds at ease, so that they would support her and stand with her.

﴿I am not one to decide a matter﴾, cutting it off or issuing a ruling that is carried out, ﴿until you bear witness﴾. The *nun* is read with a kasra; reading it with a fatha is a grammatical error (*lahn*), because the *nun* takes a fatha only in the place of raising (*raf'*), whereas this is in the place of accusative (*nasb*). Its original form is *tushhadunanī*; the first *nun* was dropped for the accusative, and the *yā'* was dropped because the kasra indicates it. With the *yā'*, both in pausal and continuous recitation, Ya'qub read it. That is: you attend me, or you advise me, or you bear witness that it is correct; that is, I do not decide the matter except in your presence. It is also said that the people of her council were three hundred and thirteen men, each of whom had command over ten thousand.

"They said, 'We are possessors of strength and possessors of great might,'" answering her. By "strength" they meant the strength of bodies and of weapons, and by "might" (ba's) they meant valour (al-najdah) and endurance in war. "But the command is yours, so consider what you will command." That is: the matter is entrusted to you, and we are obedient to you; so command us with your order and we will obey you and not oppose you. It is as though they were advising her to fight, or meant: "We are men of war, not men of opinion and counsel, while you are the possessor of judgement and management, so consider what you see, and we will follow your opinion." When she sensed from them an inclination toward fighting, she inclined toward reconciliation and arranged her reply. She first refuted what they had mentioned and showed them the error in it, where.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 34:

﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town﴾ by force and coercion, ﴿they ruin it﴾ they destroy it, ﴿and make the honored of its people the most humiliated﴾ they humiliate its honored ones, dishonor its nobles, and kill and take captives. (p-604) She thus mentioned to them the evil outcome of war. Then she said, ﴿And thus they do﴾, meaning: this is their constant custom, which does not change, because she had been in the house of the former king, so she had heard and seen things like that. Then she mentioned afterward the matter of the gift and the sound opinion she had adopted. It was also said that this is a confirmation from God of her statement. The one who seeks corruption in the land has used this verse as evidence, and whoever deems forbidden things lawful has disbelieved; and whoever uses the Qur'an as evidence in a distorted way has combined two kinds of disbelief. ﴿And indeed I am sending them a gift﴾ [al-Naml: 35], that is: I am sending messengers with a gift.

"Then (fa-nāẓiratun) — i.e., (fa-muntaẓiratun), awaiting — with what (bi-mā), i.e., bi-mā, because the alif is dropped with the preposition in an interrogative — the envoys will return," with its acceptance or its rejection. For she knew the custom of kings and the good standing of gifts with them: if he is a king, he will accept it and depart; if he is a prophet, he will reject it and will not be satisfied with us unless we follow his religion. So she sent five hundred boys dressed in the clothing of girls and their ornaments, riding horses covered with brocade, their bridles and saddles adorned with gold set with jewels; and five hundred girls on mounts, in the dress of boys; and a thousand bricks of gold and silver; and a crown crowned with pearls and rubies; and a casket in which was a virgin pearl and a jasper with a crooked hole. She sent envoys and appointed over them al-Mundhir ibn ʿAmr, as evidenced by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿with what the envoys will return﴾. She wrote a letter in the form of the gifts, and in it she said: "If you are a prophet, then distinguish between the male servants and the female servants, inform me of what is in the casket, pierce the pearl with a hole, and thread a string through the jasper." Then she said to al-Mundhir: "If he looks at you with an angry glance, then he is a king, so do not let his appearance frighten you; but if you see him cheerful and gentle, then he is a prophet." The hoopoe came and informed Solomon of the whole story. Solomon then commanded the jinn, and they struck bricks of gold and silver and spread them out in a courtyard before him, its length seven farsakhs. They made around the courtyard a wall whose battlements were of gold and silver, and he commanded that the finest animals of land and sea be brought, and they tethered them on the right and left of the courtyard upon the bricks. He commanded that the offspring of the jinn, who were a great multitude, be stationed on the right and left, then he sat upon his throne with the chairs on either side of him, and the devils arranged themselves in rows a farsakh long, and mankind in rows a farsakh long, and the beasts, the predators, the birds and the creeping things likewise. When the people drew near and saw the animals dunging upon the bricks, they threw away what they had brought of gifts. When they stood before him, Solomon looked at them with a cheerful countenance, and they gave him the queen's letter. He looked into it and said: "Where is the casket?" He commanded the termite, which took a hair and passed it through the pearl; and a white worm took the thread in its mouth and passed through the jasper. He called for water, and the maidservant took water in her hand and put it into the other, then struck her face with it, and the boy, as he took it, struck his face with it. Then he returned the gift and said to al-Mundhir: "Go back to them."

﴿When he came﴾ to Sulayman, his messenger, al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr, [the queen] said: ﴿Will you supply me with wealth?﴾ With two nuns (*nunayn*) and with the *ya'* retained both in continuous recitation (*wasl*, joining words without pause) and at pause (*waqf*, stopping at the end of a word), it is read by Makki and Sahl. Madani agreed with them, and Abu 'Amr in continuous recitation, reading *atumiddunnī*. Hamzah and Ya'qub, in both states, [read it with two nuns]. Others read it with two nuns and without *ya'* in either case. The address is to the messengers. ﴿What Allah has given me﴾ of prophethood, kingship and blessing is better than ﴿what He has given you﴾ of the adornments of this world. It is read with a *fath* on the *ya'* by Madani, Abu 'Amr and Hafs. ﴿Rather, you rejoice in your gift﴾. *Hadiyyah* (gift) is the name of the thing given, just as *'atiyyah* (grant) is the name of the thing granted. It may be attributed to the giver or to the recipient. You say, "This is the gift of so-and-so," meaning either it is the one he gave or the one that was given to him. The meaning is: what I have is better than what you have, because Allah has given me the religion, in which lies the greatest share and the widest sufficiency, and has given me from this world what cannot be increased upon. So how would someone like me be content to be supplied with wealth? Rather, you are a people who know only the outward appearance of the life of this world, and therefore you rejoice in what is added to you and sent to you as a gift, because that is the limit of your aspiration, whereas my state is contrary to yours. I am not pleased with anything from you, nor do I rejoice in it, except through faith and abandoning Magianism.

The difference between your saying "Will you supply me with wealth, when I am richer than you?" with *wa* (and) and saying it with *fa* (so) is this: when I say it with *wa*, I make my addressee aware of my increase in wealth, and yet he supplies me with wealth. When I say it with *fa*, I have made him one whose knowledge of my state is hidden from him, so I inform him right now of what I do not need in addition to his supply, as if I were saying to him, "I reject what you have done, for I am independent of it." It is in this sense that ﴿so what Allah has given me﴾ came. The purpose of the *idrab* (turning from one matter to another) is that, when she had denied them the supply and given a reason for her denial, she turned from that to explaining the cause that moved them to it, which is that they do not know the cause of contentment or joy except that a share of this world, which they know no other than, be sent to them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 37:

﴿Return to them﴾ — an address to the Messenger, or to the hoopoe, carrying another letter back to them: ﴿Come to Bilqis and her people﴾, ﴿and We shall surely come upon them with armies that they have no power (qibal) against﴾, that is, no strength to withstand them. The real meaning of qibal is resistance and confrontation, i.e., they will not be able to oppose them. ﴿And We shall surely drive them out from it﴾, from Saba', ﴿humbled, and they will be debased﴾. The humbling (dhull) is that there will leave them what they had of might and kingship, and debasement (saghar) is that they fall into captivity and disdain.

When her messenger returned to her with the gifts and related the story to her, she said: "He is a prophet, and we have no power against him." Then she placed her throne at the end of seven chambers, locked the doors, and appointed guards to watch over it. She sent to Sulayman: "I am coming to you, so that I may see what it is you call to." She set out toward him with twelve thousand qayls, under each qayl were thousands. When she reached a farsakh's distance from Sulayman—

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 38:

﴿He said, "O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?"﴾ He intended by this to show her some of the wonders that Allah Most High had granted him the power to perform at his hand, together with making her aware of the greatness of Allah Most High's power, and of what bears witness to the prophethood of Sulayman. Or he intended to seize it before she submitted, since he knew that once she had submitted it would not be lawful for him to take her property; but this is far-fetched according to the people of verification (ahl al-tahqiq). Or he intended that it be brought to him and that it be disguised and altered, and then he would look to see whether she would recognise it or deny it, in order to test her intellect.

﴿He said, "An ifrit (ʿIfrīt) of the jinn said,"﴾ — that is, the wicked, rebellious one, whose name was Dhakwān — ﴿"I will bring it to you before you rise from your place"﴾ — the place of your judgment and your judicial session — ﴿"and indeed I am over it"﴾ — over its carrying — (p-607) ﴿"strong and trustworthy."﴾ I will bring it as it is, taking nothing from it and not altering it. So Sulayman, peace be upon him, said: "I want something quicker than this."

[Al-Nasafi, *Madarik al-Tanzil*, on Surah 27, verse 40]

﴿Said the one who had knowledge of the Scripture﴾: that is, an angel in whose hand was the Book of Decrees, whom God Most High sent when the ifrit spoke. Or it was Jibril, peace be upon him. In this case the Book is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). Or it was al-Khidr, or Asif ibn Barkhiya, the scribe of Sulayman, and this is the most correct view and the view of the majority. He had the Greatest Name of God (ism Allah al-a'zam), by which when one calls, He answers. It is: "Ya Hayy, ya Qayyum, ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram," or "Ya Ilahana wa Ilaha kulli shay'in, Ilahan wahidan, la ilaha illa Anta" (O our God and God of everything, one God, there is no god but You). It was said that he had knowledge of the course of hidden things through inspiration (ilham, divine inspiration). ﴿I will bring it to you﴾: the throne. "Atika" (I will bring you) occurs in both places and may be a verb or an active participle. The meaning of His words ﴿before your glance returns to you﴾ is that you send your glance toward something, and before you return it you have seen the throne before you. It is related that Asif said to Sulayman, peace be upon him: "Extend your eyes until your glance reaches its limit." So he extended his eyes and looked toward the right. Then Asif called upon God, and the throne vanished from its place and then emerged beside the assembly of Sulayman by the power of God Most High, before his glance returned. ﴿When he saw it﴾: that is, the throne, ﴿settled beside him﴾: firmly established in his presence, not unsettled. ﴿He said: This﴾: that is, the attainment of my wish, which is the presence of the throne within the time it takes a glance to return, ﴿is by the grace of my Lord﴾ upon me and His kindness to me, without any merit on my part. Rather, it is a grace free of any return and pure of any purpose. ﴿That He may try me, whether I will be grateful﴾: that He may test me, whether I will be grateful for His favour, ﴿or ungrateful﴾. ﴿And whoever is grateful, is grateful only for his own soul﴾, because by it he lightens from that soul the burden of obligation, protects it from the mark of ingratitude, draws in more, and binds blessing to himself. Gratitude is thus a tether for an existing blessing and a snare for a lost blessing. In the words of one of them: "Ingratitude for blessing is ruin. Scattered favours seldom return to their place once they have fled. So summon the one that has strayed through gratitude, and retain the one that is present through generous companionship. Know that the full covering of God Most High soon shrinks if you do not hold God in reverence," that is, if you do not give thanks to God for His blessings. ﴿And whoever is ungrateful﴾ by abandoning thanks for the blessing, ﴿then indeed my Lord is Self-Sufficient﴾ above thanks, ﴿Generous﴾ in bestowing favour upon one who is ungrateful for His blessing. Al-Wasiti said: "What is of our gratitude is for us, and what is of His blessing is to us, and to Him belongs the obligation and the favour upon us."

**"He said, 'Disguise for her her throne'"** (﴿قالَ نَكِّرُوا لَها عَرْشَها﴾): *nakkirū* means *ghayyirū*, "change it." That is, *make its front its back and its top its bottom.*

**"we will see"** (﴿نَنْظُرْ﴾): it is in the jussive (*majzūm*, the mood that drops the final vowel) because it is in response (*'alā al-jawāb*) to the imperative *nakkirū*, which is treated as a conditional. The sense is: if you do this, we will see.

**"whether she is guided"** (﴿أتَهْتَدِي﴾): *hal tahtadī*, meaning, to the knowledge of her throne, or to the correct answer (*al-jawāb al-ṣawāb*) when she is asked about it.

**"or is of those who are not guided"** (﴿أمْ تَكُونُ مِنَ الَّذِينَ لا يَهْتَدُونَ﴾).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 42:

﴿When she came﴾ Bilqis, ﴿it was said: "Is your throne like this?"﴾ Hā (ها) is for alerting (al-tanbih), and the kāf (ك) is for comparison (al-tashbih), and dhā (ذا) is a demonstrative noun (ism ishara). He did not say "Is this your throne?" but rather "Is it like this, your throne?" so that it would not be a leading suggestion (talqin). ﴿She said: "It is as if it were it"﴾. She answered in the best of answers, for she did not say "It is it," nor "It is not it." This was from the soundness of her intellect, since she did not commit to either of the two possibilities that were open. Or, since they had made it ambiguous for her with their saying "Is your throne like this?", she made it ambiguous for them with her saying "It is as if it were it," even though she knew that it was her throne. ﴿And we were given knowledge before her﴾: this is from the speech of Bilqis, meaning: we were given knowledge of the power of God Most High and of the soundness of your prophethood through the signs mentioned earlier, concerning the matter of the hoopoe and the messengers, before this miracle, namely the bringing of the throne, or before this state. ﴿And we were Muslims﴾: submitting to you, obedient to your command. Or it is from the speech of Sulayman and his retinue, who joined their saying "And we were given knowledge of God, of His power, and of the soundness of what came from Him, before her knowledge" to her speech, or "We were given knowledge of her Islam and of her coming in obedience before her coming." ﴿And we were Muslims﴾: monotheists, humbly submissive.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 43:

﴿وَصَدَّها ما كانَتْ تَعْبُدُ مِن دُونِ اللهِ﴾ "And what she used to worship besides Allah had barred her" — it is connected to the speech of Sulayman. That is: it barred her (p-609) from knowledge of what we have known, or from advancing to Islam, namely the worship of the sun and her upbringing among disbelievers. Then he clarified her upbringing among disbelief with his words ﴿Indeed, she was from a people who were disbelievers﴾. Or it is a new independent statement, meaning: Allah the Exalted said, "And it had barred her before that from what she had entered into, her straying from the right way," or Allah or Sulayman barred her from what she used to worship, by way of omitting the preposition and making the verb reach its object directly.

﴿It was said to her, "Enter the palace."﴾ That is, the palace (*qasr*) or the courtyard of the house. ﴿When she saw it, she thought it was a deep water,﴾ a great expanse of water, ﴿and she uncovered her shins.﴾ The reading "*sa'aqayha*" with a hamza is that of Makki (Ibn Kathir). It was narrated that Solomon, before her arrival, ordered that a palace of white glass be built on her route, that water be channelled beneath it, and that fish and other creatures be placed in it. He set his throne in its centre and sat upon it, and the birds, the jinn and humankind gathered around him. He did this so that she would increase in her regard for his affair and so that his prophethood would be affirmed. It was also said that the jinn disliked his marrying her, lest she disclose their secrets to him, because she was the daughter of a jinn. And it was said that they feared he would beget from her a son who would combine the cleverness of the jinn and of humankind, so that they would pass from the dominion of Solomon to a dominion that was harsher. They said to him: "There is something wrong with her intellect, she has hair on her shins, and her foot is like the hoof of a donkey." So he tested her intellect by changing the throne (to an unfamiliar form), and he built the palace in order to see her shin and her foot. She uncovered them, and behold, she had the most beautiful shins and feet of all people, except that she had hair. Then he averted his gaze. ﴿He said,﴾ to her, ﴿"Indeed, it is a palace paved smooth,﴾ levelled and even, and from the same root comes *amrad* (beardless, smooth-skinned), ﴿made of glass."﴾ Solomon had intended to marry her, but he disliked her hair, so the devils prepared depilatory cream (*naurah*) for her, and it removed the hair. Solomon then married her and loved her, and he confirmed her in her kingdom. He would visit her once a month and remain with her for three days, and she bore him a son. ﴿She said, "My Lord, I have wronged myself,"﴾ by worshipping the sun, ﴿"and I have submitted with Solomon to God, the Lord of the worlds."﴾ The muhaqqiqun (the scholars of verification) said: it is not admissible that Solomon (peace be upon him) would devise a stratagem to look at her shins, for she was a stranger to him, and such a claim cannot be validly maintained.

﴿And We certainly sent to Thamud their brother﴾ in lineage, ﴿Salih﴾. (It is) a *badal* (substitution, i.e., apposition).

﴿That worship Allah﴾: Reading the *nun* with a *kasrah* in connected speech (*wasl*) are ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and the Basri (reader). The others read it with a *ḍammah*, following the *bāʾ* (*ittibāʿan li-l-bāʾ*). The meaning is: "that worship Allah alone." ﴿Then, behold﴾ (*li-l-mufājaʾah*, the particle expressing sudden surprise), ﴿they﴾ is a *mubtadaʾ* (subject), ﴿two parties﴾ is a *khabar* (predicate). ﴿Dispute﴾ is a *ṣifah* (descriptive clause), and it is the governing element (*ʿāmil*) of *idhā*. The meaning: "Then behold, the people of Salih are two parties: one believing in him and one disbelieving in him, disputing with one another. Each party says, 'The truth is with me.'" This is explained in His words: ﴿The eminent ones of his people who were arrogant said to those who were deemed weak, to those among them who believed: "Do you know that Salih is one sent from his Lord?" They said: "Indeed, we believe in that with which he has been sent."﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 75] ﴿Those who were arrogant said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in that which you believe."﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 76] And the disbelieving party said: ﴿"O Salih, bring us what you threaten us with, if you are indeed among the messengers."﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 77]

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 46:

﴿He said: "O my people, why do you seek to hasten the evil before the good?"﴾ That is, the punishment with which you are threatened. ﴿Before the good﴾ means before repentance. ﴿If only﴾ means "why not." ﴿You would seek forgiveness from God﴾ means you would ask for forgiveness for your disbelief by repenting and believing, before the punishment descends upon you. ﴿So that you may be shown mercy﴾ means through being answered.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 47:

﴿They said: "We have taken omen from you"﴾ meaning: we consider you a bad omen (tashā'amnā bika), because they were struck by drought at the time of his mission, owing to their denial, and they attributed it to his coming. The original form is "taṭayyarnā" (tatayyarnā), and it has also been read this way; the tā' was assimilated into the ṭā' and an alif was added because the ṭā' is vowelled with sukūn. ﴿and [you] and those with you﴾, namely the believers. ﴿He said: "Your omen is with Allah"﴾, that is: your cause, from which comes your good and your evil, is with Allah, and it is His decree (qadar) and His apportionment (qismah); or your deeds are written with Allah, so what has befallen you has befallen you only as a punishment for you and a trial. From this is the verse ﴿And every person's omen We have fastened to his neck﴾ [al-Isra': 13]. Its origin is that when a traveller passed by a bird which he would use for augury (yazjuruhu), if it passed on his right (sānihan) he took it as good fortune, and if it passed on his left (bārihan) (p-611) he took it as ill omen. Then, when they attributed good and evil to the bird, the term was borrowed for that which was their cause, namely the decree and apportionment of Allah, or the deed of the servant, which is the cause of mercy and retribution. ﴿Rather, you are a people being tried﴾, meaning: you are being tested, or you are being punished for your sin.

﴿And there were in the city﴾, the city of Thamud, which is al-Hijr, ﴿nine groups (rahṭ)﴾. Rahṭ is a collective noun with no singular, and for this reason the number nine could be specified by it, as though it were said "nine persons (anfus)". It ranges from three to ten. It is related from Abu Duraid that their leader was Qudar ibn Salif, and they are the ones who strove to hamstring the she-camel, and they were the sons of their nobles. ﴿Who spread corruption in the land and did not amend﴾. This means that their characteristic was pure corruption, not mixed with any part of righteousness, as you see some corrupters who occasionally display some righteousness. It is related from al-Hasan: they wronged the people and did not restrain the wrongdoers from wrongdoing. It is related from Ibn ʿAta: they pursued the faults of people and did not conceal their shameful matters.

They said, "Swear to one another by God" (*taqasamu*, "make a covenant with one another"). This is a *khabar* (predicate, here meaning a statement) in the position of a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause), with *qad* implied, so the meaning is: "they said while swearing to one another." Alternatively, it is an imperative: some of them commanded the others to take the oath. "Surely we will ambush him" means we will kill him by night (*bayatan*), that is, at night. "And his family" means his child and his followers. "Then surely we will say to his guardian" means to the guardian of his blood.

Ḥamzah and ʿAlī read *latubayyitunnahu* with a *tāʾ* at the beginning and a *ḍamma* on the second *tāʾ*, and *thumma latagulunna* with a *tāʾ* and a *ḍamma* on the *lām*. Ḥafṣ reads *mahlika ahlihi* ("the destruction of his family"). Abū Bakr, Ḥammād and al-Mufaḍḍal read *mahlaka*, from *halaka* (to perish): the first form, *mahlika*, is the place of destruction, and the second, *mahlaka*, is the verbal noun. The others read *muhlaka*, from *ahlaka* (to destroy), which is either the act of destroying or the place of destruction. The meaning is: "We did not confront his family, so how would we have confronted him?" Or: "We were not present at the place of his destruction, so how would we have taken charge of it?" "And indeed we are truthful" in what we have mentioned. (p-612)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 50:

﴿And they schemed a scheme, and We schemed a scheme, while they did not perceive.﴾ Their scheming (makruhum) is what they concealed of the plan to ambush Salih and his family (fatk), and the scheming of Allah (makr Allah) is their destruction from where they did not perceive. It is likened to the scheming of the schemer by way of metaphor (isti'arah).

It is narrated that Salih had a place of worship (masjid) in al-Hijr, in a ravine (shi'b) where he would pray. They said: "Salih claims that he will be finished with us within three days, so we will finish with him and his family before the third." So they went out to the ravine and said: "When he comes to pray, we will kill him. Then we will return to his family and kill them." But Allah sent a rock from the mountain-side opposite them, and they hurried away, and the rock sealed them in at the mouth of the ravine. Their people did not know where they were, and they did not know what had been done to their people. Allah punished each of them in his place, and saved Salih, peace be upon him, and those who were with him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 51:

﴿So look at the outcome of their plot, how We destroyed them and their people, all of them.﴾ With the hamza of "anna" pronounced with a fatha, (it is read) by Kufans and Sahl; with a kasra, by the others, as a new sentence (isti'naf). Whoever reads it with a fatha makes it marfu' (nominative) on the basis that it is either a substitute (badal) for "al-'aqibah" (the outcome), or the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), its estimated form being: "it is their destruction." Or he makes it mansub (accusative) on the basis of the sense (ma'na), meaning "because we..." (li-anna), or on the basis that it is the predicate (khabar) of "kana" (was), meaning: so the outcome of their plot was destruction (al-tadmir/al-dammar). ﴿And their people, all of them﴾ — by the Cry (al-sayha).

Translation:

﴿So those are their houses, ruined⌉ — ﴾ fallen and collapsed, from khawa al-najm (the star's "khawa," meaning when it falls); or empty (khaliyah) from emptiness (al-khawa'). It is a circumstantial clause (hal), and what governs it is what that demonstrative "those" indicates. ﴿Because of what they did wrong﴾ — because of their wrongdoing. ﴿Indeed in that﴾ — in what was done to Thamud — ﴿is a sign for a people who know﴾ — Our power — so that they may take heed.

Note on the rendering above: the opening ﴿ ﴾ bracket was misplaced in my draft. The correct form is:

﴿So those are their houses, fallen and collapsed, [from khawa al-najm (the star's "khawa," meaning when it falls)]; or empty (khaliyah) from emptiness (al-khawa')...﴾

Corrected translation:

﴿So those are their houses, empty﴾ — fallen and collapsed, from khawa al-najm (the star's khawa, meaning when it falls); or empty (khaliyah) from khawa'. It is a circumstantial clause (hal), and what governs it is what that demonstrative "tilka" ("those") indicates. ﴿Because of what they did wrong﴾ — because of their wrongdoing. ﴿Indeed in that﴾ — in what was done to Thamud — ﴿is a sign for a people who know﴾ — Our power — so that they may take heed.
﴿And We saved those who believed﴾ through Salih, ﴿and who used to be wary﴾ of abandoning his commands. (p. 613) They were four thousand who were saved with Salih from the punishment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 54:

﴿And [mention] Lot, when he said to his people: "Do you commit the abomination while you see [it]?"﴾ [Mention] Lot (wa-udhkur Lūṭan): "idh" is a substitute (badal) for "Lūṭan," meaning: mention the time of Lot's saying to his people, ﴿Do you commit the abomination?﴾ That is, the coming of males (ityān al-dhukūr). ﴿And you see﴾ you know that it is an abomination, not preceded by anyone (lam tusbaqū ilayhā), from: the sight of the heart (baṣar al-qalb); or [it means] that some of them see it from others, because they used to practice it in their assemblies (nādī), openly, without any of them concealing it from another, out of recklessness (majjāna) and absorption in disobedience. Or [it means] you see the traces of the sinners before you and what befell them. Then he made it explicit and said.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 55:

﴿Indeed, do you﴾ with two hamzas (read by the Kufans and the Syrians) ﴿approach men lustfully﴾ for the sake of desire ﴿instead of women?﴾ That is: Allah the Exalted created the female only for the male, and He did not create the male for the male, nor the female for the female; so such conduct is opposed to Allah in His wisdom. ﴿Rather, you are a people who are ignorant﴾, meaning you act like those who are ignorant of the fact that it is an abomination, despite your knowledge of that. Or the "ignorance" intended is the folly and wantonness in which they were. The address (khitab, direct address) and the third person (ghaybah, indirect reference) have been combined in His saying ﴿Rather, you are a people who are ignorant﴾ and ﴿Rather, you are a people who are being tested﴾ [al-Naml: 47], so the direct address was given precedence over the third person, because it is stronger, since the original principle is that speech is between those present.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 56:

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said: "Expel the family of Lut"﴾ That is: Lut and those who followed him. The predicate of "kāna" (kāna, "was") is ﴿jawāb﴾ (answer), and its subject is ﴿an qālū﴾ (that they said), ﴿from your town. Indeed they are people who purify themselves﴾, that is, they keep themselves aloof from filth. They denounce this foul act, and their denunciation irritates us. It has been said that this is mockery, like His saying: "Indeed you are the forbearing, the rightly guided" [Qur'an 11:87].

﴿So We saved him﴾: We delivered him from the punishment that befell the people. ﴿And his family, except his wife, whom We decreed﴾ (p-614) with tashdid (the doubling of the middle consonant, reading قَدَّرْناها as opposed to قَدَرْناها), as read by Hammad and Abu Bakr. That is, We decreed her existence, ﴿to be among those who remained behind﴾: among those who remained in the punishment.

And We rained upon them a rain [of stones], [stones] on which the name of their owner was written. ﴿And We rained upon them a rain.﴾ ﴿So evil was the rain of those who were warned.﴾ Those who did not accept the warning.

Wait, I should correct that: the commentary text is what I must translate faithfully, so here is the accurate rendering:

And We rained upon them a rain: stones upon which the name of each one's owner was written. ﴿So evil was the rain of those who were warned﴾, those who did not accept the warning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 59:

﴿Say: All praise is for Allah, and peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen.﴾ He commanded His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) to praise Him, and then to invoke blessings upon those chosen from among His servants, as a preface to what follows of the proof of His oneness and His power over everything. This is an instruction for every speaker, in every matter of importance, to seek blessing through these two (the praise of Allah and the salutation upon His chosen servants) and to seek support through their standing. Or, it is an address to Lot (peace be upon him), that he should praise Allah for the destruction of the disbelievers of his people, and give peace to the one whom Allah chose, rescued from their ruin and protected from their sins. ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate (with Him)?﴾ With the letter ya (يُشْرِكُونَ, "they associate") is read by Basri and ʿĀṣim. There is no good at all in what they have associated, so that it could be weighed against Him who is the Creator of everything. This is only a reproach to them and a mockery of their state. That is because they preferred the worship of idols over the worship of Allah, the Exalted. No rational person prefers one thing over another except for a motive that impels him to prefer it, such as an increase in good or benefit. So it is said to them, while knowing that there is no good in what they have preferred, and that they did not prefer it for an increase in good, but out of desire and frivolity, that they be alerted to their extreme error and the ignorance that ruined them, and that they may know that preference must be for the greater good. ("When he, peace and blessings be upon him, recited it, he would say: Rather, Allah is better, more enduring, more exalted, and more generous.") Then He, glorified be He, enumerated the goods and benefits which are the effects of His mercy and bounty, and so He said:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 27, verse 60:

﴿Is it not He who created the heavens and the earth﴾. The difference between *am* (أمْ) and *am* (أمْ) in ﴿أمّا يُشْرِكُونَ﴾ [al-Naml: 59] and in ﴿أمَّنْ خَلَقَ السَماواتِ﴾ is that the former is *muttasila* (connected, coupled), since the meaning is "which of the two is better," whereas this one is *munqati'a* (disconnected), meaning "rather" (بَلْ) together with the interrogative *hamza* (الهَمْزَةِ). (p-615) When God said, "Is what you associate better, or the gods?", He then said, "Rather, ﴿Is it not He who created the heavens and the earth better?﴾" This is to establish for them that the One who is able to create the world is better than a lifeless stone that has no power over anything. ﴿And He sent down for you water from the sky﴾, meaning rain, ﴿and We caused to grow﴾. The discourse shifts from the third person (absence) to the first person plural (speaking), to emphasise that the action belongs exclusively to Him and to indicate that producing diverse gardens, kinds, colours, flavours and shapes, all of them beautiful, from one water, is something none can do but He alone. ﴿Thereby﴾, by the water, ﴿gardens﴾, meaning orchards. A *hadiqah* is an orchard that is enclosed by a wall, from *al-ihdaq*, which is encompassing. ﴿Full of﴾ (ذاتَ): it does not say *dhawat*, because the meaning is "a group of gardens," just as one says "the women went" (ذَهَبَتْ). ﴿Of delight﴾, meaning of beauty, because the onlooker takes delight in it. Then he (al-Zamakhshari, or the author's source, implicitly) reinforced the sense of exclusivity with His words: ﴿It was not for you to cause its trees to grow﴾. The meaning of *al-kaynunah* (existence, being brought about) is *al-inbighā'* (being fitting or proper), meaning that the bringing about of that is impossible from anyone other than Him. ﴿Is there a god with God?﴾, meaning, is there another who is joined with Him and made a partner to Him? ﴿Nay, but they are a people who ascribe equals﴾, that is, they make others equal to Him, or they deviate from the truth, which is monotheism. The words ﴿Nay, but they﴾ after the address are more eloquent in rejecting their opinion.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 27, verse 61:

﴿Is He who made the earth﴾ and what follows it is a *badal* (substitution, i.e., an apposition) of ﴿Or is He who created﴾ [an-Naml: 60], so its ruling is the ruling of that [clause], ﴿a stable abode﴾. He spread it out and leveled it so that one may settle upon it. ﴿And placed within it﴾: *zarf* (adverb of place), meaning in its midst, and it is the second object, while the first is ﴿rivers﴾. And between the two seas [He placed] the like of it. ﴿And placed for it﴾, for the earth, ﴿firm mountains﴾, mountains that prevent it from moving. ﴿And placed between the two seas﴾, the sweet and the salty, ﴿a barrier﴾, preventing them from mixing. ﴿Is there a god with Allah? Rather, most of them do not know﴾ the *tawhid* (the affirmation of God's oneness), so they do not believe.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 62:

﴿Is He who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him?﴾ Al-iḍṭirār (compulsion, being driven by necessity) is an iftiʿāl form derived from al-ḍarūrah (necessity), which is the state that compels one to seek refuge. One says iḍṭarrahu ilā kadhā (he compelled him to such-and-such). The active and passive participle is muḍṭarr, and the muḍṭarr is the one whom illness, poverty, or one of the calamities of time has driven to supplication and humble entreaty to God; or the sinner when he seeks forgiveness; or the wronged person when he calls out; or one who raises his hands having no good deed of his own except tawhid, and he is in danger from it. ﴿And removes the evil﴾: the harm or the oppression. ﴿And makes you successors of the earth﴾: that is, in it, meaning your inheritance of its dwelling and your disposal of it generation after generation; or he intended by khilāfah (succession) sovereignty and dominion. ﴿Is there a god along with God? Little do you take heed.﴾ Abū ʿAmr reads "yatadhakkarūn" with the letter yāʾ, and Ḥamzah, ʿAlī and Ḥafṣ read it with the lightened form (tadhakkarūn with a single dhāl). Mā is extra (zāʾidah), meaning: you take heed, a little taking of heed.

﴿Or who guides you﴾ by the stars ﴿in the darkness of the land and the sea﴾ at night, and by landmarks on the earth by day? ﴿And who sends the winds﴾ — al-Rih (الرِيحُ, the singular form, "the wind") is the reading of Makki, Hamza and Ali. ﴿as glad tidings﴾ — bushran (بُشْرًا) is from al-bisharah (البِشارَةُ, "good news"), and this has been discussed in Surat al-A'raf. ﴿before His mercy﴾ — in front of the rain. ﴿Is there a god with God? Exalted is God above what they associate with Him.﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 64:

﴿Is He not (better) who originates the creation﴾ yunshi'u al-khalq (brings the creation into being) ﴿then repeats it﴾. It was said to them "then He repeats it" while they denied the repetition (resurrection), because their pretext was removed by granting them the capacity for knowledge and acknowledgment, so there remained for them no excuse in denial. ﴿And who provides for you from the sky﴾ i.e., the rain, ﴿and the earth﴾ i.e., from the earth, the plants. ﴿Is there a god along with Allah? Say: Bring your proof﴾ your argument for your associating (others with Him), ﴿if you are truthful﴾ in your claim that there is another god along with Allah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 65:

﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah.﴾ "Man" (مَن) is the subject (fa'il) of "yaʿlamu" (knows), and "al-ghayb" (المَغيب, the unseen, which is that for which no proof has been established and which has not been disclosed to any creature) is the object (maf'ul), and "Allah" is a substitute (badal) for "man". The meaning is: no one knows the unseen except Allah. Indeed, Allah, exalted is He, is far above being among those in the heavens and the earth, but it came in the dialect of the Banu Tamim, where they treat the disjunctive exception (al-istithna' al-munqati', i.e. an exception that is not of the same kind as what precedes it) as if it were a connected exception (al-istithna' al-muttasil), permitting both the accusative and the substitution form in the disjunctive case just as in the connected case, and they say: "There is no one in the house except a donkey."

'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "Whoever claims that he knows what will happen tomorrow has indeed committed a great slander against Allah."

And Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah.﴾

It has been said that it was revealed concerning the polytheists when they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the time of the Hour. ﴿And they do not perceive﴾ (wa ma yash'uruna), i.e. do not know, ﴿when﴾ (ayyana), i.e. when, ﴿they will be raised﴾ (yub'athuna), i.e. they will be resurrected.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 66:

﴿Rather, their knowledge has been perfected (bal idrāk)﴾ Makkī, Baṣrī, Yazīd and al-Mufaḍḍal read أدْرَكَ (adraka), meaning it ended and was completed, from أدْرَكَتِ الفاكِهَةُ (the fruit has ripened), meaning it became fully ripe. بَلِ "ادَّرَكَ" (bal "addaraka") is from al-A'shā, on the form افْتَعَلَ (ifta'ala), and بَلِ "ادّارَكَ" (bal "iddāraka") is read by others, meaning it became firmly established.
