Its original form is تَدارَكَ (tadārak), in which the tā' was assimilated into the dāl (idghām, assimilation of one consonant into another), and the alif al-waṣl (connecting alif, used at the beginning of a word to make it pronounceable) was added so that it could be pronounced. ﴿Their knowledge concerning the Hereafter﴾ means: concerning the matter of the Hereafter and its meaning. The meaning is that the causes of the firm establishment and completion of knowledge, namely that the Resurrection is certain to occur, have reached them, and they have been enabled to know it, yet they are doubtful and ignorant. This is His saying: ﴿Rather, they are in doubt concerning it. Rather, they are blind to it.﴾ The three instances of إضراب (iḍrāb, a shift from one statement to another) describe their condition and repeat their ignorance. He first described them as not perceiving the time of the Resurrection, then as not knowing that the Resurrection will occur, then as floundering in doubt and uncertainty without removing it, although its removal is possible, and then with something worse in state, which is blindness. He made the Hereafter the starting point of their blindness and its source, so he used مِن (min) rather than عَنْ (ʿan) with it, because disbelief in the outcome and the recompense is what prevented them from reflection and contemplation.

The point of connection between the content of this verse, which describes the polytheists as denying resurrection despite the firm establishment of the causes of knowledge and their ability to know, and what precedes it, which concerns God's exclusive knowledge of the unseen, is this: when He mentioned that servants do not know the unseen, this was a demonstration of their incapacity (p-618) and a description of the limitation of their knowledge. He then connected to it that they have an even greater incapacity, namely that they say of what is bound to occur, which is the time of the recompense for their deeds, that it will not happen, although they have the means of knowing that it will occur and the firm establishment of knowledge of it. It is also permissible that the description of them with the firm establishment and completion of knowledge is sarcastic toward them, as you say to the most ignorant of people, "How knowledgeable you are!" as mockery. This is because they doubted and were blind to its affirmation, whose path to knowledge is open, let alone that they would know the time of its occurrence, for which there is no path to knowledge.

It is also permissible that أدْرَكَ (adraka) means it ended and came to an end, from your saying أدْرَكَتِ الثَمَرَةُ (the fruit has reached its end), because that is its ultimate limit, at which it is annihilated. Al-Ḥasan explained it as اضْمَحَلَّ عِلْمُهم في الآخِرَةِ (their knowledge concerning the Hereafter vanished). And تَدارَكَ (tadāraka) is from تَدارَكَ بَنُو فُلانٍ (the sons of so-and-so followed one another), when they follow one another into destruction.

And those who disbelieve say: ﴿When we are dust, and our fathers, shall we indeed be brought out?﴾ from our graves as living beings. The stressing (taqrir) of the interrogative particle (harf al-istifham) in أئذا (a-idha) and أئنا (a-inna), in the reading of ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and Khalaf, is a denial upon denial and a repudiation following repudiation, and an indication of emphatic, exaggerated disbelief. The word إذا (idha, "when") is governed by ﴿لمخرجون﴾ (lamukhrajūn, "indeed brought out"), which implies the verb نُخرَج (nukhraj, "we are brought out"). This is because the active participle (ism al-fa'il) and the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul) following the interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifham), or inna, or the lam of emphasis (lam al-ibtida'), do not govern what precedes them, so how much less when these are combined. The pronoun in إنّا (inna) refers to them and to their fathers, because their being dust has encompassed them and their fathers, but the reported speech (al-hikayah) was given precedence to the absent third person. ﴿وآباؤنا﴾ (wa-ābā'unā, "and our fathers") is a conjunction (ʿatf) on the pronoun in ﴿كنّا﴾ (kunnā, "we were"), because the object has run in the manner of emphasis (tawkid).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 68:

﴿We have indeed been promised this﴾, i.e., the resurrection, ﴿we and our fathers before⁠﴾, before (the time of) Muhammad (ﷺ). Here "this" has been placed before ﴿we and our fathers﴾, whereas in Surah al-Mu'minun it is ﴿we and our fathers﴾ placed before "this", to indicate that the point of mention here is the resurrection, while in that surah the emphasis is on those who are resurrected. ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients⁠﴾: this is nothing but their tales and their lies.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 69:

﴿Say: Travel through the earth and see how was the end of the criminals.﴾ That is: the final outcome of the disbelievers. In mentioning the crime (ijram) there is a gentle warning (lutf) to the Muslims to abstain from crimes (jara'im), like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So their Lord levelled it over them for their sin﴾ [al-Shams: 14], and His saying ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned﴾ [Nuh: 25].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 70:

﴿And do not grieve over them﴾, that is, because they did not follow you and did not submit so that they would be safe. ﴿And do not be in distress﴾, that is, in tightness of chest, ﴿because of what they plot﴾, from their scheming and their stratagem against you. For indeed Allah will protect you from the people. It is said: "ḍāqa al-shay'u ḍayqan" (the thing became narrow), with a fatḥa on the ḍād, which is the reading of everyone except Ibn Kathir, and with a kasra on the ḍād, which is his reading.

Quran 27:71: ﴿And they say, "When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?"﴾ That is: the promise of punishment, if you are truthful that the punishment will descend upon the deniers. [An-Naml: 64]

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 72:

﴿Say: "Perhaps some of what you are hastening for will be close behind you."﴾ They were hastening for the promised punishment. It was said to them: "Perhaps some of it will be close behind you," and this is the punishment of the Day of Badr. The lam (ل) is added for emphasis, like the ba' (ب) in ﴿and do not cast yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195]. Or the verb is taken to imply a meaning that takes the lam, as in "danā lakum" (it drew near to you) and "azifa lakum" (it approached you), and its meaning is: it followed you and overtook you. And ʿasā (perhaps), la'alla (perhaps) and sawfa (will) in the promise and threat of kings indicate the truth and seriousness of the matter, and in this manner the promise and threat of God proceed.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 73:

﴿And indeed, your Lord is truly full of bounty﴾, meaning: bestowal of favour, ﴿upon mankind﴾, by deferring punishment from them, ﴿but most of them do not give thanks﴾. Meaning: most of them do not recognise the due right of this blessing, nor do they thank Him for it, so they hasten the punishment out of their ignorance.

Surely your Lord knows what their breasts conceal (tukinnu), that is, hide, and what they reveal (yu'linun), that is, make manifest, of speech. So the delay of the punishment for them is not because their state is hidden, but rather there is for it an appointed time; or it means that He knows what they hide and what they reveal of enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and of their schemes, and He will punish them for that with what they deserve. It is also read "takunnu" (with the first letter of the verb pronounced as "tu-kunnu"). It is said: kanantu al-shay' and aknantuhu, when I concealed it and hid it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 75:

﴿There is not an unseen thing in the heaven and earth but that it is in a clear Record.﴾ He named the thing that is hidden and concealed: ghā'ibah (unseen) and khāfiyah (hidden). The tā' in both is like the tā' in ʿāqibah (outcome) and its counterparts, al-ramiyyah (the thing shot), al-dhabīhah (the thing slaughtered), and al-naṭīhah (the thing gored), in that they are nouns and not adjectives. It is also permissible that both be adjectives, with the tā' there for emphasis (mubālaghah), as in rāwiyah (one who narrates much). It is as if he said: "There is no thing of intense concealment but that Allah knows it, encompasses it, and has recorded it in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz)." Al-mubin means the manifest, clear one, for whoever looks into it among the angels.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 76:

﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel﴾, i.e., it makes clear to them ﴿most of that about which they differ﴾. For they differed concerning the Messiah (al-Masih), and they split into factions regarding him, and mutual denunciation arose among them concerning many matters, to the extent that some of them cursed others. The Qur'an has descended with an explanation of what they differed about, had they been fair, acted upon it, and submitted, meaning the Jews and the Christians.

{وَإنَّهُ} And indeed it (i.e., the Qur'an) {لَهُدًى وَرَحْمَةٌ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ} is surely a guidance and a mercy for the believers, namely for those among them who act justly and believe. That is, among the Children of Israel, or among them and others besides them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 78:

﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them﴾ between those who believed in the Qur'an and those who disbelieved in it, ﴿by His judgment﴾ by His justice, because He only judges with justice; so the thing judged is called a "ḥukm" (judgment), or [it means] by His wisdom (ḥikmah). What supports this is the reading of those who read "bi-ḥikamihi," the plural of ḥikmah (wisdom). ﴿And He is the All-Mighty﴾ so His judgment is not repelled, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of whom He judges in favour of and of whom He judges against. Or [al-ʿAzīz means] the All-Mighty in His retribution against the falsifiers, and [al-ʿAlīm means] the All-Knowing of the separation between them and the truthful.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 79:

﴿So put your trust in Allah﴾. He commanded him to rely upon Allah and to pay little heed to the enemies of the religion. ﴿Indeed, you are upon the clear truth﴾. He gave the reason for relying upon Allah as being that he was upon the manifest truth (al-haqq al-ablaj), which is the evident religion, about which there is no doubt. In this is an indication that the one who holds the truth is worthy of trusting in Allah and of His support. (p-621)

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 27, verses 80–81:**

﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating.﴾ ﴿Nor can you guide the blind out of their misguidance.﴾ Since they did not comprehend what they heard and did not benefit from it, they were likened to the dead, though they were living with sound senses, and to the deaf who are called but do not hear, and to the blind who lose their way. No one except God Most High can remove this from them and make them guided and clear-sighted. Then He emphasized the state of the deaf with His words ﴿when they turn away, retreating﴾, because when one moves away from the caller by turning his back on him, he is even farther from perceiving his voice. "Wa-la yasma'u al-summu" (and the deaf do not hear) is read by Makki, and likewise in Surat al-Rum. "Wa-ma anta tahdi al-'umya" (nor can you guide the blind) is also read this way in Surat al-Rum by Hamzah. ﴿You can make none hear except those who believe in Our signs﴾, that is, your making them hear is of no use except for those whom God knows will believe in His signs, that is, will affirm them. ﴿So they are Muslims﴾, sincere, from His words ﴿Indeed, whoever submits his face to God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 112], meaning: makes it whole and devoted to God, purely for Him.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 27, verses 80–81:**

﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating.﴾ ﴿Nor can you guide the blind out of their misguidance.﴾ Since they did not comprehend what they heard and did not benefit from it, they were likened to the dead, though they were living with sound senses, and to the deaf who are called but do not hear, and to the blind who lose their way. No one except God Most High can remove this from them and make them guided and clear-sighted. Then He emphasized the state of the deaf with His words ﴿when they turn away, retreating﴾, because when one moves away from the caller by turning his back on him, he is even farther from perceiving his voice. "Wa-la yasma'u al-summu" (and the deaf do not hear) is read by Makki, and likewise in Surat al-Rum. "Wa-ma anta tahdi al-'umya" (nor can you guide the blind) is also read this way in Surat al-Rum by Hamzah. ﴿You can make none hear except those who believe in Our signs﴾, that is, your making them hear is of no use except for those whom God knows will believe in His signs, that is, will affirm them. ﴿So they are Muslims﴾, sincere, from His words ﴿Indeed, whoever submits his face to God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 112], meaning: makes it whole and devoted to God, purely for Him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 82:

﴿And when the word has come to pass against them﴾ He called the meaning and purport of the word "the word" (al-qawl), namely what they were promised of the establishment of the Hour and the punishment. Its "coming to pass" (wuqu') means its occurrence, and what is intended is the imminence of the Hour and the appearance of its portents, and the time when repentance will no longer benefit. ﴿We will bring forth for them a beast from the earth, which will speak to them﴾. It is the Jassasah (the Beast of the Earth). In a hadith: "Its length is sixty cubits; no seeker can overtake it and no fleeing one can escape it. It has four legs, a downy coat, feathers, and two wings." It has also been said that it has the head of a bull, the eye of a pig, the ear of an elephant, the horn of a camel, the neck of an ostrich, the chest of a lion, the color of a leopard, the flank of a cat, the tail of a ram, and the hoof of a camel, and the distance between its joints is twelve cubits. It will emerge from Safa and speak to them in Arabic, saying ﴿that the people did not believe in Our signs﴾, that is, they did not believe in my emergence, because its emergence is one of the signs. And it will say: ﴿Surely the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ (p-622), or it will speak to them of the falsehood of all religions other than the religion of Islam, or that this one is a believer and that one is a disbeliever. The Kufan reading opens "anna" (that), and it is easy on the basis of the omission of the preposition, meaning: "concerning their speech that..." Others read it with a kasra, because "speaking" carries the meaning of "saying," or because the verb "say" is implied, meaning: the beast says that, and the meaning would be: "by the signs of our Lord." Or it is a quotation of the speech of Allah the Exalted at that time. Then he mentioned the establishment of the Hour and said:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 83:

﴿And on the Day when We gather from every community a multitude﴾ — min (مِن) here is partitive (lil-tab'id), meaning: "Remember the Day when We gather from every community of the nations a band (زمرة, zumrah)" — ﴿of those who deny﴾ — min here is explicative (lil-tabyin) — ﴿Our signs﴾ — those revealed upon Our prophets — ﴿and they will be driven in ranks﴾ — their first is held back until their last, so that they gather together, and then they are driven to the place of reckoning. This is an expression for the great number, and likewise al-fawj (الفوج) is an expression for a large group.

Until, when they arrive [at the place of reckoning], they are present at the station of accounting and questioning. He (exalted is He) says to them, as a threat: ﴿Did you deny My signs,﴾ which were revealed to My messengers, ﴿while you did not encompass them in knowledge?﴾ The waw here is for the circumstantial state (al-hal), as if He said: "Did you deny My signs hastily, at first glance, without reflection or consideration that would lead to comprehensive knowledge of their reality and of whether they deserve belief or denial?" ﴿Then what was it you were doing?﴾ Since you did not reflect upon them, for you were not created in vain.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 85:

﴿And the word will come into effect against them for what they wronged, so they will not speak﴾ That is: the promised punishment will envelop them because of their wrongdoing, which is their denial of the signs of Allah. It will preoccupy them so that they cannot speak or offer an excuse, like His saying: ﴿This is a Day on which they will not speak﴾ [al-Mursalat: 35].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 86:

﴿Have they not seen that We made the night for them to rest therein, and the day to give sight?﴾ "Mubsiran" is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause). He attributed the seeing (al-ibṣār) to the day, while it belongs to its people, and the antithesis (al-taqābul) is observed in terms of meaning, because the meaning of "mubsiran" is: so that they may see therein the ways of turning about in livelihoods. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ — who affirm, and so take heed. In it is evidence for the soundness of resurrection (al-ba'th), because its meaning is: Have they not known that We made the night and the day a means of sustenance for their livelihood in the world, so that they might know that this was not made in vain, but as a trial and a test, and that there must then be reward and punishment; and if these two do not exist in this abode, then there must be another abode for reward and punishment.

And [mention] the Day when the Trumpet (al-Sur) is blown. It is a horn, or it is the plural of ṣūra (form). The one who blows it is Isrāfīl (peace be upon him). ﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified﴾. The verb fazi'a (in the past tense) was chosen over yafza' (in the present tense) to indicate that the terror is realized, established, and certain to occur. The intended meaning is their terror at the first blast, when they will be struck senseless. ﴿Except whom Allah wills﴾, that is, except those whom Allah has made firm of heart among the angels. They said: they are Jibrīl, Mīkā'īl, Isrāfīl, and the Angel of Death (peace be upon them). It was also said: they are the martyrs. It was said: the ḥūr (companions of paradise) and the guardians of the Fire and the bearers of the Throne. And from Jābir (may Allah be pleased with him): among them is Mūsā (peace be upon him), because he was struck senseless once, and [the exception applies] similarly to him. ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be struck senseless, except whom Allah wills﴾ [al-Zumar: 68]. ﴿And all will come to Him﴾. Ḥamzah, Ḥafṣ, and Khalaf read ātūhu (with the verb in the form ātūhu), while others read ātawhu, and its original form is ātiyūhu. ﴿Humbled﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial adverb), meaning: abased. The meaning of "coming" (al-ityān) is their presence at the place of standing, their return to His command, and their submission to Him, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 88:

﴿And you see the mountains, you think them﴾ with the *sin* vowelled with a *fatha*, according to al-Shami, Hamza, Yazid and ʿAsim, and with a *kasra* according to the others. It is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier, a term denoting an accusative describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) of the addressee. ﴿Fixed in place﴾, standing still and refraining from movement, from *jamada* in the sense of remaining in one place when one has not departed. And it passes by is a *ḥāl* of the pronoun in the accusative in *taḥsabuhā*. ﴿Like the passing of clouds﴾, meaning: passing as the passing of clouds does. The meaning is that when you see the mountains at the time of the Blast, you will think them fixed in one place because of their enormity, while they move at a swift pace like clouds when the wind drives them. Likewise, large bodies that are numerous, when they move, their movement is hardly discernible, as al-Nabigha said describing an army:

Against a host like a mountain, its formation so dense, one thinks they stand still for a need, while the riding camels amble.

﴿The work of Allah﴾ is a *maṣdar* (verbal noun, an infinitive-like noun) governed by what is implied by *marra* (it passes), because their passing like the passing of clouds is part of the work of Allah. It is as if it were said: Allah has done that as a work, and He mentioned the name of Allah because He had not been mentioned before. ﴿Who perfected everything﴾, that is, made His creation firm and sound. ﴿Indeed, He is Acquainted with what you do﴾, read by Makki, Basri, Ghayr Sahl, and Abu Bakr except for Yahya, and the others with the *tā'* (ta), meaning: He knows what the servants do, and He will recompense them according to that. Then he summarized that with His saying.

﴿Whoever comes with the good deed﴾, i.e., with his saying "There is no god but Allah" according to the majority (al-jumhur). ﴿Then he will have something better than it﴾, i.e., he will have a good that accrues to him from it, and that is Paradise. On this view, *khayr* does not mean "better" (afḍal), and *minhā* ("from it") is in a position of raising as a descriptive modifier of the predicate, i.e., *bi-sababihā* ("because of it").

﴿And they will be safe from terror﴾: *min faziʿin* with the Kufan reading, i.e., from a terror that is intense, extremely severe, which is the fear of the Fire. Or it means "from a terror" of any kind, however slight. And with the reading without *tanwīn* (nunation), *ghayrihim* ("other than them"). ﴿on that Day﴾: the Kufan and Madani readings, and with a kasra on the *mīm* (*yawma'idhin*), *ghayrihim*. The intended meaning is the Day of Resurrection. *Āminūn* ("secure"): *amina* is transitive through a preposition (*bi-l-jārr*) and directly (*wa-binafsihi*), like His saying ﴿Do they feel secure from the plot of Allah?﴾ [al-A'raf: 99].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 90:

﴿Whoever comes with the evil deed﴾, i.e. with shirk (associating partners with God), ﴿they will be flung, their faces, into the Fire﴾, i.e. they will be cast (ألقيت).

It is said: "kababtu al-rajul" (كَبَبْتُ الرَجُلَ), meaning: I threw the man onto his face. So the meaning is: they will be thrown onto their heads into the Fire. Or the whole (person) is expressed by the face, just as it is expressed by the head and the neck; so the meaning is: they will be thrown into the Fire. It is also said that they will be told, as a rebuke, at the moment of being thrown down: ﴿Are you being recompensed except for what you used to do﴾, in the world, of shirk and sins.

(p-625)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 91:

﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to worship the Lord of this city﴾ — Makkah — ﴿who has made it sacred﴾ — He made it a sanctuary (ḥaram) of security, in which whoever seeks refuge becomes safe; its grass may not be cut, its thorny plants may not be cut down, and its game may not be frightened away. ﴿And to Him belongs everything﴾ — along with this city — so He is the Owner of this world and the Hereafter. ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾ — those who submit (al-munqadilīn) to Him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 92:

﴿And that I should recite the Qur'an﴾: from al-tilawa (recitation), or from al-tulluw (following), as in His saying ﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ahzab: 2]. He commanded His Messenger to say: "I have been commanded that I should single out God alone for worship and not associate any partner with Him, as Quraysh did, and that I should be among the ḥunafāʾ (upright monotheists, sing. ḥanīf) who remain steadfast upon the religion of Islam, and that I should recite the Qur'an so that I may know the lawful and the unlawful and what Islam requires." He singled out Makkah from among all other lands by attributing His name to it, because it is the most beloved of His lands to Him and the greatest of them in His sight. He pointed to it with His saying "this," as a sign of its exaltation and nearness, indicating that it is the homeland of His Prophet and the descent-place of His revelation. He described His Essence with "the Sanctuary" (al-taḥrīm), which is the particular attribute of it, and He made the inclusion of everything under His lordship and dominion (malakūt) as a consequence of its inclusion under those two. ﴿So whoever is guided﴾ by following me in what I am engaged in of the Oneness of God, the negation of partners from Him, entering the upright religion (al-milla al-ḥanīfiyya), and following what has been sent down to me of revelation ﴿then he is guided only for his own soul﴾: the benefit of his guidance returns to him, not to me. ﴿And whoever goes astray, say: I am only one of the warners﴾; that is: whoever goes astray and does not follow me, then it is not upon me; I am only a warning Messenger, and upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 27, verse 93:

﴿Say: "All praise is for Allah. He will show you His signs, and you will recognize them."﴾ Then He commanded him to praise Allah for what He had bestowed upon him of the blessing of prophethood, which no other blessing can equal, and to threaten his enemies with what Allah will show them of His signs in the Hereafter, so they will then be certain of them. It is also said that it refers to the splitting of the moon, the smoke, and what befell them of the punishments of Allah in this world (p-626).

﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do.﴾ With the ta' (you, addressed to the people of Makkah) it is read by Madani, Shami, Hafs and Ya'qub, as an address to the people of Makkah; with the ya' (they) it is read by others. That is: every deed they do, Allah is knowledgeable of it and not unaware of it. Heedlessness (ghaflah) and forgetfulness (sahw) are impossible for Him.
